client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus on any of my university assignments — I'll sit down to study and just end up staring at the wall for an hour. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because it's not like anything can actually change what happened.
therapist: Losing your grandmother is a profound loss, and it makes complete sense that your mind and heart are struggling to focus on everyday things right now — grief has a way of taking up so much space inside us. You're right that nothing can change what happened, and I want you to know I'm not here to try to fix that or take the pain away, but sometimes just having a place to voice what we're carrying can help us feel a little less alone with it. I'm curious — when you sit down to study and find yourself staring at the wall, what kinds of thoughts or feelings tend to come up for you in those moments?

client: When I sit down to study, I just keep thinking about how the last time I talked to her, I was distracted and kind of rushed her off the phone because I had an exam to study for. And now all I can think is that I traded one of my last real conversations with her for... notes I don't even remember anymore. It feels like the studying itself has become this symbol of something I'm ashamed of.
therapist: That's such a painful thing to carry — the thought that you chose studying over her in that moment, and now studying itself feels like a reminder of that regret. But I gently want to reflect something back to you: you were a student trying to do your best, and you had absolutely no way of knowing that call would take on the weight it does now — that's not selfishness, that's just being human in an ordinary moment. I wonder, if your grandmother could have seen the full picture of who you are to her — not just that one rushed call, but everything — what do you think she would have said about the kind of person you are?

client: I've thought about that before, actually — what she would have said — and part of me wants to believe she'd be kind about it, because she always was. But then another part of me thinks I'm just telling myself what I want to hear, like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. It feels almost dishonest to imagine her forgiving me when I haven't really forgiven myself yet.
therapist: That tension you're describing — between what you sense is true and what you feel you deserve to believe — is actually a really important and honest insight, and it shows a lot of integrity that you're not just reaching for easy comfort. But I'd gently invite you to consider: is it possible that self-forgiveness isn't about "letting yourself off the hook," but rather about holding yourself with the same kindness your grandmother always offered you — the kindness you clearly learned from her? What do you think it would actually mean for you to forgive yourself here — what would that look like, or feel like?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, the idea of holding myself the way my grandmother held me... that actually caught me off guard a little, because it doesn't feel like something I've ever really considered. But I think the honest answer is I don't even know what forgiving myself would look like — like, would I just stop replaying that last visit in my head, stop wishing I had stayed longer or said more? It almost feels like if I stop feeling guilty, I'm somehow saying it didn't matter, that she didn't matter, and I can't bring myself to do that.
therapist: What you just named is so important — you've been holding onto the guilt almost as a way of honoring her, as if the pain is proof of how much she mattered to you. But I wonder if there's another way to look at it: what if the fact that you loved her so deeply, that you *care* this much about one rushed phone call, is already the most powerful testament to how much she mattered — and that you could carry her memory with love and gratitude rather than guilt, without that meaning she mattered any less? What do you think she would have wanted to be remembered through — your suffering, or something else?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're probably right — she wouldn't have wanted me to be miserable. But it's not that simple, because if I let go of the guilt, it almost feels like I'm letting go of her, like I'm saying that last phone call didn't matter. I know that sounds irrational, but the guilt is the thing I reach for when I miss her, and I don't know what I'd replace it with.
therapist: It doesn't sound irrational at all — it sounds like guilt has quietly become your way of staying close to her, a bridge back to her when the missing feels unbearable, and of course you'd hold onto that. But what strikes me is that you've just described something really significant: that the guilt is actually standing in for connection, for love, for grief — and I wonder if there might be other ways to reach for her that could hold that love without the pain of self-blame, whether that's a memory, a ritual, or something she passed on to you that lives in who you are. What's something about her — a quality, a saying, a moment — that you'd want to carry forward as a way of keeping her close?

client: That's... a really different way of looking at it, and part of me wants to push back because the guilt feels so automatic, like it just happens to me rather than something I'm choosing. But when you ask about a quality she had... she was the kind of person who always noticed when someone was struggling before they said a word, she had this quiet way of just showing up. I guess I do that too sometimes, and I never really connected that to her before.
therapist: What a beautiful thing to discover in the middle of so much pain — that she is already living on in you, in the way you show up for others, in that quiet attentiveness you didn't even realize you'd inherited from her. And I notice you said the guilt feels automatic, like it just *happens* to you — that's actually a really important observation, because in my experience, the things that feel most automatic are often the ones most worth gently examining, since they're usually thoughts we've never had the chance to consciously choose. When you imagine showing up for someone else the way she showed up — with that quiet, noticing presence — do you think you'd offer them the same harsh judgment you've been giving yourself?

client: No, I wouldn't judge them that way — I know I wouldn't. If a friend came to me and said they hadn't visited someone enough before they died, I'd probably hold them and tell them that love doesn't get measured in visits. But when it's me, it's like... that same logic just doesn't apply, and I don't fully understand why I can't extend myself the same thing.
therapist: You just said something really profound — you already *know* the truth, you can feel it clearly enough to offer it to someone else, and yet there's this wall that stops it from reaching you, and that gap between what we know and what we can feel for ourselves is one of the most deeply human struggles there is. What you're describing has a name in CBT — it's called a double standard, where we hold ourselves to a harsher judgment than we'd ever apply to someone we love, and just noticing that it's happening is genuinely the first step toward softening it. I'm wondering — what do you think it would feel like, even just for a moment, to imagine yourself as the friend in that scenario, and let yourself receive the same words you'd so naturally offer to them?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, part of me gets it intellectually — like, yes, double standard, that makes sense on paper. But when I actually try to imagine being the friend in that scenario, receiving those kind words... it just feels wrong, almost uncomfortable, like I'm trying to wear clothes that don't fit me. I think there's this deep part of me that genuinely believes I don't deserve the same compassion, and I'm not sure just imagining it differently is going to change that feeling.
therapist: That discomfort you're describing — the feeling that self-compassion just doesn't fit — is such an honest and courageous thing to name, and I want you to know that's not a sign this work isn't for you, it's actually a sign we've found something really important worth exploring together. You're right that simply imagining it differently won't instantly change a belief that's likely been with you for a long time, and I'd never want to suggest healing is just a matter of thinking the right thoughts — real change tends to happen slowly, in small moments, not all at once. I'm curious — can you think of where that belief might come from, the one that says you don't deserve the same compassion you'd give others, because I wonder if your grandmother's loss is the loudest thing right now, but perhaps not the only thing this is connected to?

client: I think it probably goes back further than my grandmother, honestly. Growing up, I always felt like I had to earn my place in the family — like love was something you got when you did things right, not just because you existed. So the idea that I'd deserve kindness just for being human, without having to justify it somehow... it genuinely feels foreign to me, almost uncomfortable to even say out loud.
therapist: What you just shared took real courage, and it makes so much sense now — if love always came with conditions growing up, then of course unconditional self-compassion would feel foreign, almost suspicious, like something that couldn't possibly be meant for you. Your grandmother sounds like she may have been one of the rare people in your life who offered you something closer to that unconditional kind of love, which might be part of why her loss feels so devastating and why that last phone call carries so much weight. I want to sit with what you've just named for a moment — what was it like to say that out loud just now?

client: Saying it out loud felt... strange, like I was hearing it for the first time even though some part of me must have already known it. There's this weird mix of relief and then almost immediately this guilt, like I'm being disloyal to my parents by admitting that my grandmother gave me something they didn't. And honestly, I'm not sure I fully trust what I'm feeling right now — sometimes in these sessions things feel very clear in the moment and then I walk out and it all just kind of dissolves.
therapist: That mix of relief and guilt makes complete sense — you're not betraying your parents by acknowledging a truth about your own experience, you're just finally letting yourself see something clearly, and that can feel both freeing and frightening at the same time. And I really appreciate you naming that worry about things dissolving afterward, because that's such an honest and self-aware thing to notice — insights often do feel fragile at first, like they need time and repetition to really take root, which is why what we're doing here is a process rather than a single moment of clarity. I'm wondering — is there one small thing from today, even just a single sentence or image, that you'd want to try to hold onto this week, something you could perhaps write down so it doesn't slip away?
